title: Pooran's Unbeaten 70 and Kenjige's Three-For Demolish the Knight Riders in Oakland
excerpt: Nicholas Pooran anchored MI New York's 144 with an unbeaten half-century, then Nosthush Kenjige — the Hyderabad-born left-arm spinner who grew up in the American cricket system — tore through LA Knight Riders' batting to bowl them out for 103 at the Oakland Coliseum.
body:
Nicholas Pooran has done many extraordinary things on a cricket field, but what he is doing in Oakland this week might be the most quietly devastating stretch of his career. For the second time in three days, the MI New York captain walked out to the middle at the Oakland Coliseum, measured the pitch, and simply refused to get out — and for the second time, the LA Knight Riders had no answer.

On Saturday afternoon, Pooran's unbeaten 70 off 58 balls was the spine of MI New York's 144 for 6 after being put in to bat. It was not the most explosive innings of the MLC season, but it was one of the most composed — a captain's knock in the truest sense, played on a surface that offered enough to make every other batter on both sides look ordinary.

## A slow build, then a Pooran eruption

The Knight Riders won the toss and chose to bowl, and for a while it looked like a shrewd call. MI New York's top order stuttered, and the powerplay yielded little. But Pooran, batting with the unhurried authority that has defined his MLC career, waited for his moments. They came in the death overs.

In the 16th over, he launched Ali Khan over the boundary for six. In the 17th, Andre Russell — as fine a death bowler as exists in T20 cricket — was taken for back-to-back sixes. In the 19th, he punched Jason Holder for consecutive fours to finish on 70 not out. Russell's figures of 4 for 35 told one story; Pooran's 70 told a more important one.

The Trinidadian had scored 62 not out against the same opponents just two days earlier. In two innings against the Knight Riders, he has now made 132 runs without being dismissed.

## Kenjige's quiet brilliance

If Pooran provided the runs, Nosthush Kenjige provided the theatre. The 34-year-old left-arm spinner — born in Auburn, Alabama to a family with roots in Karnataka’s Chikkamagaluru district, now one of the most experienced cricketers in the American system — bowled with the kind of control that makes T20 batting look far harder than it should be.

Kenjige finished with 3 for 21 from his four overs, strangling the Knight Riders' middle order and ensuring the chase never gained traction. His dismissals were textbook: flight, dip, turn, and enough variation to keep even experienced international batters guessing.

For MI New York, the Indian-American spinner has been the unsung constant. While the headlines go to Pooran and Trent Boult, Kenjige's economy and wicket-taking in the middle overs have quietly been among the most valuable contributions of the season.

## Knight Riders crumble for 103

The chase was never alive. Andre Fletcher made 44 off 40 balls — a defiant but ultimately lonely effort — and Colin Munro contributed 20 before being run out in the seventh over when a moment of miscommunication cut short the only partnership that threatened to build momentum.

Once Kenjige and Boult (who was again miserly with the new ball) applied the squeeze, the Knight Riders folded. The last six wickets fell for 32 runs as MI New York's bowling unit hunted as a pack. The innings ended in the 18th over, 103 all out — 41 runs short of the target and, more importantly, a long way short of the form a team needs to survive a tournament this tight.

## What it means for the Bay Area

This was MI New York's second win over the Knight Riders in three days at the same ground. The first, an eight-wicket demolition in which Pooran scored 62 not out and Monank Patel made 56, had already put LA Knight Riders on the brink. Saturday's result may well have pushed them over it.

For the Bay Area's desi community, the significance runs deeper than standings. The Oakland Coliseum — the sprawling East Bay arena that has hosted baseball legends and football dynasties — is now, improbably, a cricket ground. MLC's decision to bring multiple matches to Oakland has turned the venue into a weekend destination for South Asian families across Silicon Valley, San Francisco, and the East Bay. Walk through the concourse during an MLC match and you will hear Punjabi, Telugu, Tamil, and Hindi before you hear English.

Kenjige, born in the United States to an Indian family, is in many ways the embodiment of that audience — a cricketer who belongs to both worlds. That he is thriving in a tournament designed to bring the sport to American soil, at a venue minutes from one of the largest Indian diaspora communities in the country, feels like something more than coincidence.

**MI New York 144/6 in 20 overs** (Nicholas Pooran 70* off 58 balls; Andre Russell 4/35) beat **LA Knight Riders 103 all out in 17.5 overs** (Andre Fletcher 44 off 40; Nosthush Kenjige 3/21) **by 41 runs** at the Oakland Coliseum, Oakland.

*Sources: MLC official data, Cricbuzz, ESPN Cricinfo*
